record.name: Sharded matrix multiplication and result ownership
record.role: Derive the communication operation from the partitioned matrix axis and the next consumer’s required result layout.
record.description: A compiler must preserve both a tensor’s values and who owns them. Splitting matrix output rows gives different ranks independent output rows; splitting the contracted inner dimension gives each rank only part of every output sum. Those are different meanings of a local matrix product, even if the local arrays have similar shapes. JAX’s explicit sharding example forms local products and then reduces their partial sums. A sum all-reduce makes the completed result available at every rank. Reduce-scatter instead finishes the sum while distributing different output pieces, and all-gather can later assemble those pieces when a consumer needs a replica. Concatenating unfinished partial sums does not perform their missing arithmetic. This distinction connects tensor-axis information in a compiler to the collective scheduled over the network. It also prevents allocating replicas merely because the preceding stage happened to use all-reduce. A valid next operator may consume distributed rows directly, while another needs a different layout and an explicit conversion. The example below uses exactly representable small integers; its equality does not imply arbitrary floating-point reduction trees are bitwise identical.
mechanism: Declare C = AB, the complete tensor shapes, stored element size and required consumer ownership before partitioning.
Split the inner dimension into disjoint sets Kᵣ; each rank receives matching columns of A and rows of B.
Compute Cᵣ locally. Each Cᵣ covers all output coordinates but contains only the products indexed by Kᵣ.
Add contributions with matching output coordinates. Use all-reduce for replicated C or reduce-scatter for completed disjoint output shards.
Retain row shards when the next operation can use them; all-gather only when the consumer requires the whole tensor.
Check every output against a separate dense reference, and count a sent payload once at its chosen link boundary. Input distribution, temporary buffers and protocol overhead are additional costs.

science.title: Inner-dimension partition preserves the sum
science.equation: Cᵣ[i,j] = Σk∈Kᵣ A[i,k]B[k,j]; C[i,j] = Σr Cᵣ[i,j]
science.explanation: The disjoint Kᵣ sets cover the contracted dimension exactly once. Each rank contributes to the same output coordinates.
science.assumptions: Exact real arithmetic or the small integer example; floating-point summation order can change rounding. No duplicated or omitted contracted indices.

science.title: Two-rank payload ledger
science.equation: Qreduce-scatter = 8 bytes/rank; Qall-gather = 8 bytes/rank; Qcombined = 16 bytes/rank
science.explanation: For this explicitly described two-rank, 2×2 float32-output schedule, each phase sends one two-element row per rank.
science.assumptions: Logical payload sent by each rank in this chosen exchange; excludes initial input placement, headers, retransmission, local reads/writes and actual collective implementation details.

record.engineeringExample: Use A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]]. Rank 0 owns k=0 and forms C₀ = [[5,6],[15,18]]; rank 1 owns k=1 and forms C₁ = [[14,16],[28,32]]. Reduce-scatter with row ownership sends C₀ row 1 [15,18] from rank 0 to rank 1, and C₁ row 0 [14,16] in the opposite direction. Rank 0 adds [5,6]+[14,16]=[19,22]; rank 1 adds [15,18]+[28,32]=[43,50]. Each sends 8 payload bytes if elements are float32. If both consumers need all of C, all-gather exchanges these completed rows for another 8 bytes sent per rank. Both then hold [[19,22],[43,50]]. Total sent payload is 16 bytes per rank, 32 across the two senders; counting the matching receives again would double-count this network boundary. Concatenating the two original 2×2 partial matrices would create four rows and would leave their sums unfinished.
record.learningObjective: Reconstruct the same 2×2 product from inner-dimension shards, choose a collective from output ownership, and reconcile the two-rank payload ledger.
record.misconception: A shard can be an unfinished contribution to every output, not necessarily a disjoint piece of the finished output.

check.question: Each rank computed all output coordinates using a different half of the contracted dimension. Is concatenating those local arrays enough?
options: No: matching coordinates still require a sum
Yes: more rows complete the dot products
Yes: any collective performs the missing multiplication
check.explanation: The local arrays are partial sums over different k indices. Reduce them before choosing replicated or sharded ownership.

checks.question: After the stated reduce-scatter, which row belongs to rank 1?
checks.explanation: Rank 1 combines both partial contributions to the second output row.

checks.question: How many payload bytes are sent across both ranks in the two stated phases?
checks.explanation: Two ranks each send 8 bytes in each of two phases. The same received bytes are not added again.

record.whyAI: Distributed linear layers become correct only when the compiler and runtime finish the same tensor operation and deliver its expected ownership. Avoiding an unnecessary replica can also save memory and communication.
record.tradeoff: A shard-preserving collective may save result replication, but a later consumer can reintroduce an all-gather or resharding cost. Logical bytes alone do not predict network latency.
record.evidenceNotes: The sources establish sharding and collective semantics. All matrices, the two-row exchange schedule and byte counts here are synthetic. This is not an observed NCCL implementation, a topology model or a performance comparison.
